Down from the funeral at the plot beside Pike's, at the back right (errata 99 G).

LOOK_AT.say: Ezra Pike. The man I was sent to find. Six years.
repeat: A plain board, kept upright. The undertaker's work, and paid for, I would guess, by the undertaker.
I have his letter of introduction in my coat. It introduces me to this.

LISTEN_TO.say: Nothing. I have come a very long way to hear it.
repeat: Nothing, still. He was never going to answer, and I keep asking anyway.
Wind in the grass over him, and that is all the reply there is.

overrides.TALK_TO: I read him my letter of introduction. It seemed only right. He took it as well as anything else I've said here.
overrides.USE: It's in use. That's the entire and only thing a plot can be.

LOOK_AT.say: A rail fence down one side of the hill, as far as the gate.
repeat: Split rails, pegged rather than nailed, and every peg tight. Somebody walks this fence.
It runs from the gate to the edge of the hill and stops, as if it had made its point.
then: The other sides are left to good manners.

LISTEN_TO.say: Wind in the rails, a low hum with no tune in it. I've looked for one.
repeat: A rail ticking as the night cools it. It's the only thing up here keeping time.
Nothing. Up here even the fence is careful how loud it is.

overrides.PUSH: It holds. The undertaker maintains it. His clients do not leave, but their reputation for it must be kept up.

LOOK_AT.say: The undertaker, at Grievance's head in his good apron.
repeat: He keeps not looking at me, which is very nearly the same thing as looking at me.
He has a hand on her bridle. She allows it, the way she allows weather.
then: He is the only man here who knows the coffin is empty, and he is sweating for both of us.

LISTEN_TO.say: He is murmuring to the mule. It sounds like an apology.
repeat: His boots shift on the gravel. He would like to be anywhere else, the box included.
Nothing. He has stopped murmuring. It was not working.

then.speaker: procession_undertaker
then.line: She's never carried an empty box up this hill. I don't know how she can tell.

then: I know exactly how she can tell.
repeat: Nine years, sir, and she has never once stopped at this gate.
TALK_TO.sceneLine: docs/110-act-three-scenes.md::### THE LINES · **TALK TO THE UNDERTAKER**

overrides.PICK_UP: He is holding the mule. Somebody has to.

LOOK_AT.say: Reverend Sowerby, with his book open at the place, ready to see me off.
repeat: There is a pencil behind his ear, for the counting.
He has not looked at me once. The clergy see the soul, and I am wearing a hat.

LISTEN_TO.say: He is turning pages to find his place, and finding it twice.
repeat: He hums the opening of a hymn under his breath, to see if it still fits.
Nothing. He is saving it.

TALK_TO.say: Reverend. Can a hill be blessed?

then.speaker: procession_sowerby
then.line: A hill? Anything can be blessed, sir. There is a rate.

TALK_TO.sceneLine: docs/110-act-three-scenes.md::### THE LINES · **TALK TO REVEREND SOWERBY**, while stalled, before the prayer

TALK_TO.say: He is mid-prayer, with his eyes shut and the whole town's shut with him. I have never had a better chance at anything.
TALK_TO.sceneLine: docs/110-act-three-scenes.md::### THE LINES · **TALK TO REVEREND SOWERBY**, while the prayer runs

LOOK_AT.say: A grave, open, waiting, with my name on the marker. Frame has spelled it wrong.
repeat: The spade is still in the spoil heap, waiting for a decision that has already been made.
Frame's spelling is on the marker in paint. The undertaker has left room to correct it, and will not.
A trickle of dirt into the bottom of it. Practice.
Nothing yet, for the second time. The yet is doing a great deal of work.

LOOK_AT.say: My plot, my headboard, HE TUNED. I visit.
repeat: The grass has started over it. I am the first man in Consolation to watch his own grave come in.
Someone has left a tuning peg on the headboard, a piano's. I know whose piano. I'm not going to say.
then: It is restful, in the way of problems that have been filed.

LISTEN_TO.say: Wind in the oats. My grave is the only one here whose tenant can review the accommodations, and I give it high marks.
repeat: Nothing. Not from me, and I'd know.
The oats again, and somewhere down the hill, a piano, in tune.

hotspots.name: PIKE'S NEIGHBOR

WALK_TO.say: The funeral is waiting on the mule. So am I.

USE.say: The funeral is waiting on the mule. So am I.

OPEN.say: The funeral is waiting on the mule. So am I.

hotspots.note: Errata 91 E: PIKE'S NEIGHBOR before it opens -- docs/110-act-three-scenes.md::### THE LINES.

LOOK_AT.say: A marker for Obadiah Mott, erected by public subscription in the fifth year. Well kept.
repeat: The flowers are wax. The undertaker's lilies, on loan for the look of the thing.
It is the best-kept grave on the hill, for a man nobody here ever buried.
Nothing under it, still.
Wind across the stone. It has a lot of town to cover and it starts here.

LOOK_AT.say: Half the town, in black, at the gate.
repeat: They are standing the way people stand at a stopped coach, politely, looking at their watches.
Not one of them has looked at me twice. A low hat does more than I would have guessed.
then: Nobody here has buried me before, and they would like to get it right.

LISTEN_TO.say: Somebody says I was a quiet sort of fellow. Somebody else says I was new.
repeat: A watch being wound, and then a second watch, out of sympathy.
Somebody asks whether the mule always does this. The undertaker says she has never done it before. Everybody looks at the coffin.
then: They agree that will be it.

TALK_TO.say: One of them tells me it is a shame about the piano man, and asks whether I knew him. I say not well.
repeat: Another tells me he was very quiet. I agree with her. I was.
TALK_TO.sceneLine: docs/110-act-three-scenes.md::### THE LINES · **TALK TO THE MOURNERS**

overrides.PICK_UP: They have come to carry me. It would confuse things to carry them.

LOOK_AT.say: Grievance, in black harness, standing at the gate as if it were a wall.
repeat: She has carried every coffin in Consolation up this hill. She has never once been fooled, and she does not mean to start with mine.
Her ears are flat. The livery man would call it professional.
then: Her head is turned toward the hearse.

LISTEN_TO.say: A long breath out through the nose, aimed at the coffin.
repeat: Her harness creaks as she shifts her weight. She shifts it away from the hill.
Nothing. She has said what she has to say.

TALK_TO.say: I tell her, very quietly, that I am not in there. She knows.

overrides.PULL: She considers the request, declines it, and goes on looking at the coffin.
overrides.PUSH: From behind? At a funeral? I would be the second thing they buried.
overrides.PICK_UP: She is in harness, and in no mood.

LOOK_AT.say: My coffin is inside, behind the glass.
repeat: Black lacquer, brass lamps and a plume on the roof. I have never traveled in such style, and I am not traveling now.
The rear of the hearse shuts on a latch. It is the kind of latch that assumes nobody inside will want out.
then: The curtains are drawn, out of respect for a man who isn't there.

LISTEN_TO.say: The coffin shifts an inch every time the wind leans on the hearse.
repeat: The brass lamps creak on their brackets whenever the wind comes over the hill.
Not a sound out of the coffin. That is the whole problem.
then: It weighs nothing, and she knows it.

USE.say: Not with half the town watching. A man climbing into his own coffin draws a crowd, and I already have one.

then.line: Grievance went through the gate before the amen.

then.speaker: thad
then.line: Behind us, Reverend Sowerby asked the Lord to look kindly on this creature, and opened his eyes to find the creature gone.

then.speaker: thad
then.line: It was a smoother ride than the stagecoach. I recommend it to anyone, at the end.

ELIAS CRANE. SURVEYOR. 1850.

exits.name: THE GATE

LOOK_AT.say: The gate, and the whole town lit up below it. From up here Consolation looks as if it knows what it's doing.
repeat: Two posts, a crossbar, and half a gate hung on one side. Nobody up here has ever needed the other half.
The path goes down through it toward the lights. I've walked it more often than most of the residents ever will.

LISTEN_TO.say: Wind through the gateway, carrying a little of the town up the hill with it.
repeat: The half gate knocking against its post, once, when the wind remembers it.
The town below, too far off to make out, and close enough to know it's there.

overrides.CLOSE: It swings back. The latch is broken in the direction of welcome, which is not the direction you want a graveyard broken in.

exits.note: Doc 20 and errata 43: Boot Hill is reached by the map, and its gate leads back to it. Doc 49's CLOSE is its one line. NO DOCUMENT WRITES THE GATE A LOOK OR LISTEN (doc 54: 'THE GATE is the room's exit'), so it is a stub exit as the records room's door is (errata 72 F, doc 36 Q157); the gate works, and its LOOK and LISTEN wait for lines. Errata 189: its LOOK and LISTEN are doc 106's (linesFrom), and it is no longer a stub.

exits.note: Doc 20: Room 31, the funeral, is reached from Boot Hill once the executor is named (E6). The open plot beside Pike is where it is held, so from E6 until the funeral is done the plot is the way up to it; its words stay on PIKE'S NEIGHBOR, which is hidden meanwhile (errata 99 G). Errata 233 (doc 110 section 2, THE WAY ON): from E6 until the ride (T_RODE_UP) the procession is stalled at the gate, and the way up refuses with doc 110's line; the ride itself is how he gets there.

say: The service is over. Mr. Pike has been remembered, six years late and very thoroughly. The town is coming back down the hill, Colonel Fanshawe in front, holding his hat.

lines.line: It's the only day you have it.

lines.line: He looks at the collection plate for a long time. Then he counts out of it with his eyes shut.

lines.speaker: sowerby
lines.line: Nine funerals of linen. He starches with feeling.
